title: Subqueries, Set Operations, and CTEs
what_is_it: A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another query - in WHERE (to compare against a computed value), or with IN (to test membership in a computed list). UNION/UNION ALL/INTERSECT/EXCEPT combine two queries' result sets like set operations. A CTE (WITH ... AS ...) names a query so you can reference it later, often more readably than an inline subquery.
why_it_matters: These are the tools for questions a single flat SELECT can't answer on its own: 'above the average,' 'in both of these lists,' 'in this list but not that one.' A CTE in particular becomes essential once a query gets complex enough that nesting subqueries directly would be unreadable.
common_mistakes: Mismatching the number or type of columns between the two sides of a UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT - both sides must return the same number of columns in compatible types, or Postgres rejects the query outright. Also reaching for a correlated subquery (which re-runs per outer row) when a plain JOIN or window function would compute the same answer faster.
mini_exercise: Predict the difference between 'SELECT customer_id FROM orders EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM appointments' and the same query with the two sides swapped - are they the same set, or different?
postgres_note: Postgres's EXCEPT is the SQL-standard name for what some other databases (MySQL historically) call MINUS - the behavior is identical.
